title: Yes, Writing Does Advance Thinking
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler, co-author of a book on advancing thinking through writing, answers a New York Times guest essay by Williams College professor Joe Cruz claiming that the evidence for writing as the highest cultivation of thought is thin. She first summarizes the case: writing moves information into long-term memory, forces the why, how and example questions that deepen understanding, and leaves a visible record that exposes incoherence. She then argues that Cruz separates learning from thinking even though cognitive science shows they are inextricably linked, and that the 2016 review he cites actually reports a consensus that writing contributes significantly to learning. His seminar example works, she suggests, because he has already written about the material, and his own students did write their topic, thesis and outline before using AI. Her main worry is that K-12 teachers will use the essay to skip writing instruction, and she closes with Louisiana teachers who found that teaching students to write clearly taught them to think clearly.
points: Writing is a stronger thinking tool than talk precisely because it is harder: it demands precision, leaves a visible record and slows us down enough to reflect.
Learning and thinking are inseparable, so conceding that writing helps learning while denying it helps thinking does not hold up.
The research Cruz cites in fact reports a consensus that writing contributes significantly to learning, especially when students are taught writing strategies and have background knowledge.
Cruz's students still did the core intellectual work of topic, thesis and outline, and the oral exam gave them a reason to do it, so his case is weaker than it looks.
The practical risk is that teachers of struggling writers read the essay as permission to drop writing, when explicit instruction reduces the cognitive load that makes writing hard.
quotes: But writing is more powerful because it’s harder. It requires more precision and clarity.
Writing also serves as a visible record of our thinking. That means that when our ideas are incoherent or fragmentary, writing makes those problems more obvious.

The big caveat is that the task of writing itself is extremely cognitively demanding. If students are overwhelmed by the cognitive load of writing, they won’t have the capacity to get the learning benefits writing can bring.
In fact, evidence from cognitive science establishes that learning and thinking are inextricably linked: the more we learn about a topic, the better able we are to think critically about it.
Of course, as others have pointed out, if Plato hadn’t written down Socrates’ criticism of writing, we would have no idea he’d ever said it.
Maybe he’s able to flit from idea to idea with such agility in oral discussion only because he’s had the experience of writing about those ideas in the past.
And they were probably motivated to do those things because they knew they would have to defend their essays in an oral exam.
We realized that when we taught our students to write more clearly, they became able to think more clearly.
